items.title: Quality assurance and quality control are different things
items.claim: A car plant inspects every vehicle at the end of the line and rejects defective units. Which approach is this?

options.text: Quality assurance, because it ensures quality
Quality control — defect detection after the fact. Quality assurance builds quality into the process so defects don't arise

items.reveal:
W. Edwards Deming, who worked in postwar Japan, argued that inspecting defects out is more expensive than preventing them. His '14 Points' for management (1986) included 'cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality'.

Toyota's andon-cord system stops the line whenever a worker sees a problem — quality is built upstream. Quality control still happens, but as a back-stop, not the main mechanism. ISO 9001 audits processes (assurance), not products (control).
items.why: Two firms with identical defect rates can have very different cost structures depending on whether defects are prevented or caught.

items.title: Patagonia's owner gave the company to the planet
items.claim: In September 2022, Yvon Chouinard announced he was transferring ownership of Patagonia. What was the structure?

options.text: An IPO on the New York Stock Exchange
All voting stock to the Patagonia Purpose Trust (climate-aligned governance); all non-voting stock (98%) to the Holdfast Collective, with future profits funding environmental causes
A sale to a private equity buyer

items.reveal:
Chouinard, his wife Malinda and their two children transferred Patagonia (valued around $3bn) using two vehicles: the Purpose Trust holds voting control to ensure mission alignment; the Holdfast Collective (a 501(c)(4) nonprofit) holds economic ownership and receives roughly $100m of annual profits to fund environmental work.

The structure required the family to pay $17.5m in gift tax. The company is a B Corp (certified since 2011) — the legal structure goes much further than B Corp certification alone.

B Lab's B Corp movement, launched in 2006, certifies firms meeting social and environmental performance standards.
items.why: Corporate ownership structures shape objectives. A trust-owned firm doesn't have to maximise shareholder returns — because its 'shareholders' are not the same as a public company's.

items.title: Market research said the Walkman would fail
items.claim: Sony launched the TPS-L2 Walkman in 1979. What did market research suggest beforehand?

options.text: Strong demand from young consumers — supporting the launch
Likely failure: consumers reported they wanted recording capability, not just playback, and disliked the absence of speakers
No research was conducted because Akio Morita had no money for it

items.reveal:
Co-founder Masaru Ibuka wanted a portable player so he could listen to opera on long flights. Akio Morita, despite hostile focus group findings, championed the launch. Sony hedged by initially offering it with two headphone jacks (so you could share) and a 'hotline' button to talk to a companion — both later dropped.

First-month sales in Japan were 30,000 units. By the early 1980s the Walkman was a global phenomenon and 'walkman' became a generic word for portable cassette player.

Clayton Christensen later used the case in 'The Innovator's Dilemma' to argue that existing customer research can't reliably predict demand for genuinely new products.
items.why: Market research has methodological limits. Consumers can tell you what they want among options they already know; they're worse at imagining a category that doesn't exist.
